intro.title: About Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios
intro.lead: Welcome to **Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios**, widely recognized as **Parque de los Dinosaurios de Orizaba** (the Orizaba Dinosaur Park). Located in the heart of **Orizaba**, **Veracruz**, **Mexico**, this destination serves as a primary hub for travelers visiting the region and a favorite stop for family holidays.
intro.landmarkCluster: When visiting **Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios**, you can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including the adjacent **Parque de las Sonrisas** and the city landmark **Teleférico de Orizaba**.
intro.description: Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios is located in Orizaba, Veracruz, Mexico. It is an amazing theme park featuring realistic dinosaur models, interactive exhibits, and family-friendly entertainment facilities. Here, you can travel back to the Jurassic era and experience the charm of dinosaurs up close. If you are looking for things to do with kids in Orizaba or across Veracruz, this dinosaur park is one of the best-recognised family options in the region; before you set off, check ticket prices, opening hours and directions in the sections of this guide.

route.overview: Discover the ideal route to explore Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios and experience the charm of the prehistoric world.
steps: Arrive at the park entrance in the morning and get a map and visitor guide at the visitor center.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Common questions about Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios (Orizaba Dinosaur Park), answered.

items.q: Where is Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios located?
items.a: Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios is located in Orizaba, Veracruz, Mexico, at Priv. de Circunvalación, Colonia Agrícola Moctezuma, 94345.

items.q: What are the opening hours of the dinosaur park?
items.a: The park is generally open Thursday to Sunday from 10:00 to 22:00 and closed Monday to Wednesday; holiday schedules may differ. Please confirm the latest hours before your visit.

items.q: How much does it cost to enter the Dinosaur Park in Orizaba?
items.a: Admission rules may change with the season or events. According to Orizaba's official tourism guide, local residents enter free with a valid official ID, while other visitors typically pay an admission fee (about MXN 150, often including neighbouring attractions such as Casavegas and Parque de las Sonrisas). Please confirm current prices on site.

items.q: What can I see at Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios?
items.a: The park displays large, lifelike reproductions of Jurassic dinosaurs created by different artists, including the Tyrannosaurus rex, Diplodocus, Spinosaurus and Triceratops, with educational information next to each model.

items.q: Is Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios suitable for children and families?
items.a: Yes. The park is designed for family outings and combines fun with education, making it very popular with children and school groups.

items.q: How do I get to the dinosaur park in Orizaba?
items.a: The nearest major airport is Veracruz International Airport (VER), about 1.5 to 2 hours away; from there take a long-distance intercity bus to Orizaba and then a short taxi ride. From central Orizaba, taxis and local buses reach the park easily, and driving with navigation also works well.

items.q: What attractions are near Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios?
items.a: Right next to the park is Parque de las Sonrisas, and the Eco parque Cerro de la Escamela is close by. City highlights such as the Teleférico de Orizaba (cable car to Cerro del Borrego) and the Palacio de Hierro are also easy to combine with your visit.

seasons.title: Seasonal Visit Strategy
seasons.subtitle: Orizaba sits in a tropical highland: temperatures stay mild all year, so rain and crowd flow are what truly shape your visit. This overview follows long-term climate records from Mexico's national weather service (SMN/CONAGUA) and is a general guide only - always confirm with the live forecast above.

items.weather: Mostly dry and sunny; mild 20-27°C by day, cooler mornings and evenings, occasional early fog.
items.crowd: Quieter weekdays after the holiday season - great for slow visits and photos.
items.tip: Add a light layer for mornings and evenings; daytime sun grows stronger, so use sunscreen.

items.weather: Temperatures climb noticeably with stronger afternoon convection; from late May rain turns more frequent, mostly short thunderstorms.
items.crowd: Numbers rise ahead of the summer break; weekends get lively.
items.tip: Visit in the morning when possible; carry an umbrella and sunscreen and wear light, quick-drying clothing.

items.weather: The wettest months of the year, with frequent afternoon storms; the air feels fresh but the ground turns slippery.
items.crowd: Peak family season; queues for kid-friendly attractions run longer.
items.tip: Check the day's storm window, pack rain gear and spare shoes, and follow guidance during thunderstorms.

items.weather: October stays humid; from November it turns drier, sunnier and pleasantly cool.
items.crowd: Year-end festivals and Christmas lights draw bigger crowds.
items.tip: Dress in layers; plan transport and parking early on festive dates.

items: Spend the morning in the main exhibition area while light is soft and crowds are small.
Have lunch in the park or at a nearby eatery, avoiding the midday sun.
Slow down in the afternoon for the interactive and family-play areas.
Revisit your favourite models before closing for final photos.

items.name: Families with children
items.desc: Centre the day on children's pace and curiosity: start with big, easy-to-recognise dinosaurs such as T. rex and Triceratops, then try the simulated digs, weaving short explanations between activities.
items.note: Tip: pack water, wipes and sunscreen, and keep a light rain poncho handy for afternoon showers.

items.name: Photography & nature
items.desc: Go at opening or just before closing, when light is softest and crowds are thinnest, for wide shots and model details; with extra time continue to the nearby hillside ecological park.
items.note: Tip: use a wide lens for panoramas and a telephoto for details; respect site rules when using tripods at busy times.

items.name: Low-effort & accessible route
items.desc: Walk the flat main loop at an easy pace and focus on the highlights of the main exhibition area; confirm accessible restrooms and wheelchair routes on site.
items.note: Tip: split the visit into short legs with rest breaks; if someone has limited mobility, take a taxi to shorten walking distances.

science.title: Dinosaur Science Corner
science.subtitle: Get to know the 'stars' of the exhibition: their real eras, sizes and ways of life.

items.title: Did they all live in the Jurassic?
items.content: Not at all. Dinosaurs appeared in the Late Triassic about 230 million years ago and vanished at the end of the Cretaceous about 66 million years ago - roughly 165 million years of dominance. The exhibits actually cover several geological periods.

items.title: Tyrannosaurus rex: apex predator of the latest Cretaceous
items.content: T. rex lived at the very end of the Cretaceous (about 68-66 million years ago); adults reached about 12 metres in length and around 7 tonnes, with one of the strongest bite forces among land animals.

items.title: Triceratops: the horned plant-eater
items.content: Triceratops lived in the same era and on the same continent as T. rex, using its neck frill and three horns for defence. It was one of the most common herbivores of the latest Cretaceous.

items.title: Diplodocus: the Jurassic 'long-neck'
items.content: Diplodocus lived in the Late Jurassic about 150 million years ago. With an enormous neck and tail it could reach over 25 metres in length, travelling in herds and feeding on high vegetation.

items.title: Spinosaurus: a fishing dinosaur that swam
items.content: Spinosaurus lived in the mid-Cretaceous and carried a tall sail on its back. It is among the longest meat-eating dinosaurs known, and research suggests it hunted fish near the water's edge.

items.title: About the models: where do the replicas come from?
items.content: The exhibits are lifelike models created by artists following scientific restoration: the skeleton is rebuilt from fossils first, then muscles and skin are added. They are educational displays, not real fossils.

responsibility.title: Education & Visitor Responsibility
responsibility.subtitle: Everyone doing their part keeps this open-air science classroom safe and pleasant for all visitors.
items: Never climb, lean on or shake the exhibit models, and do not press against barriers - protect the displays and yourself.
Do not cross barriers into staged areas; children should stay under adult supervision.
In open-air areas, protect yourself from the sun and stay hydrated; during thunderstorms follow on-site guidance and shelter nearby.
Dispose of litter in bins or carry it out to help keep the park clean.
Do not write on or carve exhibits and facilities, and respect no-smoking signs where they apply.
Rules on pets, cycling and drones may vary - please follow the park's current notices.

historyTimeline.title: History & Significance of Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios

items.title: From Ahuilizapan to Orizaba
items.description: The valley that hosts the dinosaur park belonged to the Nahuatl-speaking world before the arrival of the Spanish. The city name comes from the Nahuatl Ahuilizapan, meaning 'place of pleasant waters', later adapted into Spanish as Orizaba. The town grew along the historic royal road between Mexico City and Veracruz.

items.title: The Circunvalación recreation belt and the dinosaur zone
items.description: In the 21st century, Orizaba's local government kept building public recreation areas along Priv. de Circunvalación, adding one themed park after another. Expo Parque de los Dinosaurios is the dinosaur-themed zone of this park belt, right next to family facilities such as Parque de las Sonrisas.

items.title: Artists' lifelike dinosaurs
items.description: The 'dinosaurs' here are not real fossils but life-size models created by artists following palaeontological restoration, from Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops to Spinosaurus and Diplodocus. Each exhibit carries an educational note, blending art and science.

items.title: A landmark of Orizaba, a Magical Town
items.description: After Orizaba earned Mexico's 'Pueblo Mágico' (Magical Town) title, its tourism facilities kept improving. Today the dinosaur park is a signature spot for family and science outings, joining icons such as the Teleférico de Orizaba and the Palacio de Hierro.

historyTimeline.guideContent: When visiting, you can start with the **main exhibition area** to admire realistic dinosaur models; then participate in activities such as archaeological digging in the **interactive experience zone**; next, have a meal and rest at the **rest area**; finally, select dinosaur-themed souvenirs at the **souvenir shop** to leave wonderful memories.
